title: MVCC
description: Understand Multi-Version Concurrency Control, comparing PostgreSQL and MySQL implementations, and explore snapshot isolation.

segments.text: Traditional locking makes readers block writers and writers block readers. MVCC, Multi-Version Concurrency Control, eliminates this. Readers never block writers, writers never block readers. Let's see how.

The core idea: instead of modifying data in place, create a new version for every write. Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot of the database as of its start time. Old versions are kept until no transaction needs them.

PostgreSQL stores all versions directly in the table heap. Each row has xmin, the transaction that created it, and xmax, the transaction that deleted or updated it. A new version creates a new physical row.

When you read a row, PostgreSQL checks: is xmin committed and started before my snapshot? Is xmax either empty or from a transaction not yet visible to me? If both conditions are true, the row is visible.
Think about the consequences of this design.
segments.thought_prompt: If PostgreSQL keeps old versions in the main table, what happens to storage over time with frequent updates?

segments.text: Bloat. Dead tuples accumulate. PostgreSQL runs VACUUM to reclaim space from rows no longer visible to any transaction. Autovacuum does this automatically, but misconfigured autovacuum is one of the most common PostgreSQL performance issues.

MySQL InnoDB takes a different approach. It updates rows in place and stores old versions in a separate undo log. The undo log is a chain of previous versions. Reads follow the chain to find the version matching their snapshot.

PostgreSQL: no undo log needed, simpler crash recovery, but table bloat requires vacuum. MySQL: in-place updates avoid table bloat, but long undo chains slow reads and the undo log itself needs purging. Different trade-offs, same goal.

Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a consistent view as of its start. It prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads. But it allows write skew, where two transactions read overlapping data and make conflicting updates.

Write skew example: two doctors check that at least one doctor is on call, then both go off call simultaneously. Each sees the other still on call in their snapshot. Result: nobody is on call. Serializable isolation prevents this.

segments.thought_prompt: When would you choose serializable isolation over snapshot isolation? What is the performance cost?

segments.text: Serializable adds conflict detection overhead and more aborts. Use it for correctness-critical operations like financial transfers. Use snapshot isolation for read-heavy workloads where write skew is unlikely. MVCC is the backbone of every modern relational database.
